APPLICATION FOR STAY OF DEMAND

Brief Facts of the Order and Demand of Tax

1. The subject appeal has been filed under cover of our letter DT 2345 dated December 9, 2022 under 
section 131 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 [Ordinance] against the Appellate Order dated 
November 23, 2022 of the Commissioner Inland Revenue (Appeals-I) [CIR(A)]. 

2. The Order of the CIR(A) disposes off the appeal filed against the Order dated January 29, 2021, framed under section 122(5A) of the Ordinance by the Additional Commissioner Inland Revenue [ACIR], 
Audit – I, Range - B, Large Taxpayers Office, Karachi [hereinafter referred as Impugned Order] where demand of Rs 88,405,132 was maintained on “exparte basis”.
Recovery Proceedings 
3. Recovery proceedings have been initiated by the Deputy Commissioner Inland Revenue, Zone-II, Range-B, Unit 04, Large Taxpayer Office, Karachi and the appellant has been served with a notice dated September 11, 2024, issued under section 138(1) of the Ordinance requiring the payment of demand of 
Rs 88,405,132 by September 12, 2024; copy enclosed as Annexure ‘A’.

4. Since the tax demanded is required to be paid by September 18, 2024, this stay application is being filed and it is prayed that the stay be granted to the appellant till the appeal has been heard and order is passed by the ATIR as the recovery proceedings would cause undue hardship for the appellant as the demand has been incorrectly adjudged for the reasons detailed in the following paragraphs.

Status of Stay from Revenue Authorities

5. Currently, no stay application is pending before any Revenue Authority or Other Authority.

Reasons for the Stay 

6. The CIR(A) has framed the Impugned Order without taking into account the submissions on merit / facts involved on the issues in appeal which were available on record; thus, the Appellate Order, made on an ex-parte basis, is illegal and warrants to be annulled. The details of proceedings are discussed below.
7. Brief facts of the proceedings are as under:

Additional Commissioner Inland Revenue

(a) Amendment proceedings for the year were initiated were initiated vide Show cause notice dated December 2, 2020, issued under section 122(5A) of the Ordinance.

(b) This required certain information / explanations with an intention to amend the assessment deemed under section 120(1) of the Ordinance. This notice was responded vide letter DT 3322 dated January 21, 2021.

(c) The above response was followed by another response vide letter DT 3527 dated January 29, 2021, after discussions with the ACIR on January 26, 2021. No new notice was received after the show cause notice dated December 2, 2020, and the Amended Order dated January 29, 2021, was framed under section 122(5A) of the Ordinance. 

Commissioner Inland Revenue (Appeals)
(d) Stay was applied and allowed by the CIR(A) on March 15, 2021. Stay application included submissions on legal and fact plaints of the disallowances made in the Amended Order dated January 29, 2021, which were made available to the CIR(A). 
(e) Hearing of appeal was fixed vide notices dated March 11, 2021, March 15, 2021, March 11, 2022, and November 15, 2022, on IRIS portal of the FBR; these were not served physically.
(f) On November 23, 2022, the subject Appellate Order was uploaded on IRIS on an ex-parte basis. Again, this Order was also not physically served at the registered address of the appellant.

Factual Submissions on the Impugned Order:
8. Addition has been made for an amount of Rs 337,273,000 under section 39 of the Ordinance considering the same as ‘Interest Income’ chargeable to tax as ‘Income from Other Source’ vis a vis declared exempt income of Rs 1,431,729,540 under Clause 141 of Part I of Second Schedule to the Ordinance. This is as under:

Taxation of Profit on Debt under Section 39 of the Ordinance as “Income from Other Sources”

ENGRO ELENGY TERMINAL (PRIVATE) LIMITED [EETPL]

TAX YEAR 2017

Ground of Appeal No. 3 

	

The ACIR has erred in subjecting the ‘Profit on debt’ of Rs 139,985,000 to tax under the head ‘Income from Other Sources’ under section 39 of the Ordinance.

	

	

ACIR’s Contentions



Reference is made to note 1 to the Financial Statements of EETPL for the year ending December 31, 2016 [copy enclosed as Annexure ‘A’] and paragraph 8.1 of the response made vide letter DT 3322 dated January 21, 2021 to show cause notice dated December 2, 2020 wherein the business of the entity has been described as that of establishment and operation of an LNG terminal. 



On this premise, it is adjudicated that since earning interest income was never a business of the taxpayer, hence markup income earned on bank deposits and term deposits is chargeable under 
section 39 of the Ordinance as “Income from Other Sources” as opposed to the treatment of the appellant, wherein such income has been charged to tax under section 18 of the Ordinance as “Income from Business”.  



The ACIR has invalidated the explanation provided that the said interest income was earned on idle funds available with the company as were kept with the bank to reduce the financial burden on the Subordinated loan from the Holding Company i.e. M/s Elengy Terminal Pakistan Limited [ETPL] by stating that:



“vi. The taxpayer’s contention that it has earned interest business income while obtaining subordinated loan from holding company is not tenable. Obtaining subordinated loan and keeping in bank is not the business of the taxpayer or it does not qualify the taxpayer for the provisions of section 18(2) of the Ordinance; rather the loan was obtained for deriving business income from operations of LNG terminal and such business income is also exempt from tax u/cl. 141 of Part of the Second schedule to the Ordinance not for the earning ‘Profit on Debt’. It is general business practice that the owner or shareholder sometimes provides equity injection and sometimes provides loan injection to its business in times of need. This does not mean that the business of the owner or the shareholder is lending money. The business of lending money in Pakistan requires certain regulatory formalities (such as banking under the Banking Companies Ordinance 1962 and compliance with prudential regulations) which are missing in this case.”





Further, the ACIR has rejected the explanation that accruing of such interest income was inevitable in pursuance to “Accounts Agreement” executed with respect to the Foreign Borrowing from IFC / ADB and local syndicate obtained during the tax year under assessment. The ACIR’s comments are as reproduced follows:



“viii. Furthermore, the taxpayer argument and reliance on Accounts Agreement (Annex A) (through which the taxpayer company is required to open and maintain only specified security accounts bearing profit/ interest) too is not tenable argument. The nature of an item of income and its taxability is determined as per provisions of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 which is not subservient to any such agreement between 2 private companies. Accordingly, the provisions/ requirements of the Accounts Agreement do not have any effect on the nature and character of any income as determined by Income Tax Ordinance, 2001. Accordingly, this argument is rejected.”





Reference has been made to sections 7B, 18(2) and 18(4) of the Ordinance, wherein profit on debt is considered “Income from Business” where the person’s business is to derive such income. In this respect, the ACIR has stated that person’s income from borrowing and lending money to the general public as in the case of Banking entities only shall be treated as “Income from Business”, therefore, any such interest income on bank deposits and term deposits is taxable as “Income from Other Sources” under section 39 of the Ordinance.



Reliance is placed on the following decisions of the appellate fora:



UCH Power (Pvt.) Ltd. and others versus Income Tax Appellate Tribunal and others cited as 2010 PTD (SC) 1809; 



Commissioner of Income Tax versus Khairul Hayat Amin and Co. Ltd. Cited as (2000) 81 TAX 311 (HC Karachi); and



Genertech Pakistan Ltd. And Other versus Income Tax Appellate Tribunal of Pakistan Lahore and Others reported as 2004 PTD 2255.





Appellants’ Arguments

		

At the outset, we state the contentions of the ACIR on subjecting ‘Profit on debt’ earned on bank deposits and term deposits of Rs 139,985,000 to tax under the head ‘Income from Other Sources’ under section 39 of the Ordinance in the Order and our counter-arguments in brief as follows: 



S.No.

ACIR’s Contentions

Explanation of facts of the case







i

“……Taxpayer’s declarations at note 1 to its audited financial statements and at para 8.1 to its reply strengthens departmental point of view that the taxpayer deals in earning business income from operation of elegy terminal and other allied activities. Furthermore, the taxpayer corporation was found to establish and operate LNG terminal etc. It was not established to earn interest income on Term Deposits, Saving Certificates and receivables. The earning interest income was never a business of the taxpayer. Hence, markup income is chargeable to tax as other income u/s 39 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 and consequently only expenses paid in earning of such income are admissible u/s 40 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001. Furthermore, the following arguments strengths this proposition:”



i. The charging provisions related to taxation of ‘profit on debt are:



“7B. Tax on profit on debt. (1) Subject to this Ordinance, a tax shall be imposed, at the rate specified in Division IIIA of Part I of the First Schedule, on every person, other than a company, who receives a profit on debt from any person mentioned in clauses (a) to (d) of sub-section (1)of section 151.



(2) The tax imposed under sub-section (1) on a person, other than a company, who receives a profit on debt shall be computed by applying the relevant rate of tax to the gross amount of the profit on debt.”

The Officer has failed to appreciate the requirements of the financing arrangements of the entity for the establishment and LNG Terminal operations of the Company. 



Details of such financing agreements alongwith profit on debt earned thereon are discussed in paragraphs 2 to 11.







ii to v

“ii. The above provisions have excluded taxation of profit on debt earned by the companies. Second important provisions related to taxation of ‘profit on debt’ are those mentioned in subsections (2) & (4) of section 18 of the Income Tax Ordinance 2001.



(2) Any profit on debt derived by a person where the person’s business is to derive such income shall be chargeable to tax under the head “Income from Business” and not under the head “Income from Other Sources”.



(4) Any amount received by a banking company or a non-banking finance company, where such amount represents distribution by a mutual fund 6[or a Private Equity and Venture Capital Fund] out of its income from profit on debt, shall be chargeable to tax under the head “Income from Business” and not under the head “Income from Other Sources”.



iii. The law contained in subsection (2) of 
section 18 of the Ordinance ibid reproduced as above clearly provides that any profit on debt derived by a person where the person’s business is to derive such income shall be chargeable to tax under the head “Income from Business”. This means that a person’s income from borrowing and lending money to the general public or indifferent clients in the open market shall be treated as income from business u/s 18 of the Ordinance ibid.



iv. Sub-section (4) of section pertains to the case of a banking company or non-banking finance company whereby their income from ‘profit on debt’ shall be treated as business income.



v. Therefore, profit on debt not falling under sections 7B, 18(2) and (18(4) of the Income Tax Ordinance 2001] is to be taxed under 
section 39(1)(c) of the Income Tax Ordinance 2001. The deductions for income falling under section 39(1) of the Ordinance ibid are allowable u/s 40 of the Ordinance.”

The issue as identified above needs to be considered in the context of the financing arrangements of the Company which include:



Subordinated loan from parent entity i.e. ETPL.



Foreign loan financing from IFC / ADB and local syndicate.



Under the above said agreements, the profit on debt earned on balances kept with banks was inevitable and hence construed as business income on basis that the loans obtained relate specifically to the financing of the business of the terminal operations of the entity.







vi to vii

“vi. The taxpayer’s contention that it has earned interest business income while obtaining subordinated loan from holding company is not tenable. Obtaining subordinated loan and keeping in bank is not the business of the taxpayer or it does not qualify the taxpayer for the provisions of section 18(2) of the Ordinance; rather the loan was obtained for deriving business income from operations of LNG terminal and such business income is also exempt from tax u/cl. 141 of Part of the Second schedule to the Ordinance not for the earning ‘Profit on Debt’. It is general business practice that the owner or shareholder sometimes provides equity injection and sometimes provides loan injection to its business in times of need. This does not mean that the business of the owner or the shareholder is lending money. The business of lending money in Pakistan requires certain regulatory formalities (such as banking under the Banking Companies Ordinance 1962 and compliance with prudential regulations) which are missing in this case.



vii. Further, the taxpayer is not lending and borrowing money from the general public but is keeping idle money in bank accounts/ making short term investments. This is done on call as a shareholder or owner rather than as a business exercise. Therefore, as per note 1 to audited standalone financial statements of the taxpayer taxpayer’s business is own and operate LNG terminal and such allied works. Hence, taxpayer’s income from profit on debt is its “Income from Other Sources” taxable u/s 39 of the Ordinance ibid.”

Again, this whole premise is based on a presumption. The facts of the Profit on Debt earned on bank deposits and term deposits and its related finance cost are necessarily required to be adjusted there against have been discussed in paragraphs 2 to 11 and Ground of Appeal no.4.







viii

“viii. Furthermore, the taxpayer argument and reliance on Accounts Agreement (Annex A) (through which the taxpayer company is required to open and maintain only specified security accounts bearing profit/ interest) too is not tenable argument. The nature of an item of income and its taxability is determined as per provisions of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 which is not subservient to any such agreement between 2 private companies. Accordingly, the provisions/ requirements of the Accounts Agreement do not have any effect on the nature and character of any income as determined by Income Tax Ordinance, 2001. Accordingly, this argument is rejected.”

The ACIR’s comments on the foreign loan agreement disregards the requirement of maintaining specific bank accounts bearing interest under the said agreements.





During the tax year under assessment, the taxpayer, EETPL had obtained a Long Term Foreign Borrowing from IFC / ADB and local syndicate in relation to the LNG Operations of the company. The said foreign loan is in addition to the subordinated loan that was received by the entity from its parent ETPL in the tax year 2015. 



The loans as obtained for the set up and financing of the LNG terminal operations is apparent from the balance sheet of the Company as depicted below: 



 

The related notes 16 and 18 to the Financial Statements are as follows:	





                     





Therefore, the profits earned on bank deposits and term deposits represent income earned on:



“Idle funds” available with the company as were kept with the bank to reduce the financial burden on the Subordinated loan from the Holding Company; and

 

Designated bank accounts as required under the “Accounts Agreement” entered into in pursuance of the Common Terms Agreement [CTA] for the foreign loan borrowing. 

	 	

	

Under the contract of financing of the foreign long term loan, the Company is required to open and maintain only specified security accounts bearing profit / interest as the prevailing rates of such accounts. The relevant provision 3.12 of the “Accounts Agreement” is depicted below for your perusal:









It is informed that the said loan was secured for the operations of the LNG Terminal. The same is apparent from the contents of the “Accounts Agreement” which show the relationship to the Floating Storage Regasification Unit [FSRU] an integral part of the Terminal under an Agreement with the non-resident Excelerate Energy Development DMCC [Relevant extracts from the “Accounts Agreement” enclosed as Annexure ‘B’]. Further, the finances so provided are confined for the purposes of the Terminal project development; detailed budgeting of which is provided as part of Contract of Financing i.e. CTA.



Moreover, the accounts so maintained include the FSRU standby letter of credit [SBLC] account; the facility being availed from the bank for purposes of compliance with credit support requirements under Time Charter Party agreement with Excelerate Energy Middle East, LLC [EE]. We give below a picture of the relevant extracts of the contract for clarity: 





 

           











         





	

	

	

Hence, markup incomed earned on bank deposits of Rs 139,985,000 has been construed as part of “Income from Business” under section 18 of the Ordinance. Consequentially the finance income of Rs 139,985,000 was set off against the total finance costs of Rs 794,882,000 as appearing in the ‘Statement of Comprehensive Income’ for the period and which relate wholly and exclusively for the purpose of financing the operations of the entity and, therefore, considered claimable against the said markup income. 



The ACIR has, however, disregarding the financing arrangements of the business of the entity, classified “Profit on Debt” as well as the fact that the related Finance Cost Rs 483,401,279 is to be allowed has subjected the Income of Rs 139,985,000 under section 39 of the Ordinance, holding tax at 31 percent applicable.



Your honour would appreciate that the action of considering this income as part of income under section 39 of the Ordinance i.e. “Income from Other Sources” and not under section 18 as “Income from Business” is not in line terms of the financing arrangements of the entity whereby the accruing of such interest income on the funds obtained through the loan arrangements is inevitable.



The decisions relied on whilst classifying finance income under section 39 of the Ordinance alongwith our rebuttals are made hereunder:



S.No.

Case Law



Rebuttal









(1)

UCH Power (Pvt.) Ltd. and others versus Income Tax Appellate Tribunal and others cited as 2010 PTD (SC) 1809



The Supreme Court of Pakistan has in this case rescinded the petitioners view of treating income generated from interest / profit received on bank accounts as exempt on account of specific exemption available under relevant law for “profits and gains” derived from electric power generation projects. 



Hence, interest income so earned has alternatively been classified as “Income from Other Sources”.



In this respect, it is contended that this case law does not relate to the issues under consideration i.e. the classification of interest income earned on bank and term deposits which has been classified as “Income from Business” of the entity taxable under section 18 of the Ordinance based on the financing arrangements of the entity.



This case is particularly applicable on entities classifying their incomes from other sources as exempt under specific provisions of the law pertaining to exemption of incomes and is hence not per se applicable here.  









(2)

Commissioner of Income Tax versus Khairul Hayat Amin and Co. Ltd. Cited as (2000) 81 TAX 311 (HC Karachi)



The Sindh High Court has in this case treated interest income earned by the assessee on loan advanced to an associate under the head “Income from Other Sources” as against “Business Income” due to insufficient evidence of nature of the entity’s business as regards to money-lending activities.   



The reason for disallowance of interest income earned by way of lending to associates / subsidiaries as “Business Income” in this case is inapplicable on EETPL.



As discussed above in the preceding paragraphs, we reiterate that income of Rs 139,985,000 pertains to profit on bank deposits and is required to be set off against the finance cost on Subordinated and foreign loan



This fact is evident from the extracts of the financial statements of the Company and notes thereto which have been reproduced and discussed in detail as above. 

 

Such interest income is hence considered income from business chargeable to tax under section 18 of the Ordinance.



The case law referred strictly pertains to interest income earned by way of loans advanced to an associate.









(3)

Genertech Pakistan Ltd. And Other versus Income Tax Appellate Tribunal of Pakistan Lahore and Others reported as 2004 PTD 2255



In this judgment it was held that interest income is chargeable to tax as income from other source and not as business income unless earning interest income was the business of the taxpayer, however, in the captioned case the main business income of the assessee was to “derive profits and gains from Electric Power Generation Project”. 



This case law yet again relates to exemption claimed by the taxpayers on their business incomes as allowed under specific provisions of the law.  



The case law hence referred is irrelevant since the classification of interest income earned on bank and term deposits as “Income from Business” is on account of the terms of financing of the entity’s operations.





Prayer



From the aforesaid, it is prayed that the basis of taxation of Profit on bank and term deposits of Rs 139,985,000 in the return i.e. after set off of the related “Finance Cost” of Rs 483,401,279 under section 18 of the Ordinance on basis of nature of long term borrowings of the entity be reinstated. 








Ground of Appeal No. 4



The ACIR has erred in not appreciating that the related finance cost of Rs 483,401,279 is not adjustable against the “Income” of Rs 139,985,000 subjected to tax under section 39 of the Ordinance.



ACIR’s Contentions



The ACIR has disallowed adjustment of related finance costs of Rs 483,401,279 against Profit on Debt of Rs 139,985,000 reclassified under section 39 of the Ordinance as “Income from Other Sources” on the premise that the finance costs have been incurred to earn exempt income under clause 141 of Part I of the Second Schedule to the Ordinance and thus are not allowed set off against income chargeable to tax i.e. interest income after reclassification. The ACIR’s remarks are as follows:



“x. The taxpayer has claimed that if its income from profit on debt is classified as ‘Income from business’; then deductions u/s 40 of the Ordinance are allowable as it has paid finance cost on the amounts lent by it; vide para 6.1 (b) of the taxpayer’s reply. The deductions allowable for “Income from Other Sources” (profit on debt) taxable u/s 39 are to be claimed u/s 40 of the Ordinance ibid.



xi. The taxpayer’s claim against fails on both factual and legal planes:



a. The taxpayer deals in deriving business income from operations of LNG terminal;



b. The loans were obtained for that purposes, i.e. to earn business income from LNG terminal operations and,



c. The finance cost incurred for loans obtained to earn/ derive business income are business expenses and allowable against only business income u/s 28(1) of the Ordinance.



d. The finance cost paid/ (payable) by the taxpayer does not fall under the classification of deduction u/s 40 of the Ordinance because the subordinated loan was not availed for earning profit on debt/ ‘Income from Other Sources’; but for deriving business income from operations of LNG terminal which is exempt from tax u/cl. 141 of Part of the Second schedule to the Ordinance. This proposition has been established by the Hon’ Supreme Court of Pakistan in the judgment of Utch Power (Pvt) Ltd cited as 2010 PTD (SC) 1809 & by the Hon’ Sindh High Court in the case of Khairatul Amin; cited as (2000) 81 TAX 311 (HC Karachi),= (2000) PTD 363.”





Following decisions of appellate authorities have been relied:



Commissioner of Income Tax versus Khairul Hayat Amin and Co. Ltd. Cited as (2000) 81 TAX 311 (HC Karachi);



UCH Power (Pvt.) Ltd. and others versus Income Tax Appellate Tribunal and others cited as 2010 PTD (SC) 1809; and



Genertech Pakistan Ltd. And Other versus Income Tax Appellate Tribunal of Pakistan Lahore and Others reported as 2004 PTD 2255.



[The summaries of decisions (i) to (iii) referred to in this Ground have been detailed in Ground of Appeal No. 3 above and based on the facts of accrual of the interest income on bank deposits, the same are considered inapplicable on such income]





Appellants’ Arguments



Your honour would appreciate as explained in the preceding Ground of appeal, that the appellant Company had entered into loan arrangements with its financiers whereby the entity was required to maintain designated Security Accounts bearing profit / interest.



It is, therefore, established that the profits accrued on bank and term deposits of Rs 139,985,000 were unavoidable in order to fund the business operations of the entity and are hence classified as “Income from Business” under section 18 of the Ordinance. 



Accordingly, the resultant finance costs incurred of Rs 483,401,279 on the loans so obtained are to be set off against the finance income earned on the loaned funds under provisions of section 28 of the Ordinance. Breakup of the related finance costs is given below:

483,401,279

 



Consequently, that is the treatment which is reflected in the return whereby the said income was set off against the related transactional and other costs associated with the subordinated and foreign loan and net finance costs of Rs 649,405,000 i.e. after set off of total finance costs of Rs 794,882,000 with mark-up income of Rs 139,985,000 and income on short term investments of Rs 5,492,000 as given below:





	

	

In view of the above and the action of the ACIR of reclassifying the finance income as “Income from Other Sources” under section 39 of the Ordinance, we are of the opinion that the finance costs of Rs 483,401,279 be then allowed adjustment under section 40 of the Ordinance since the same are directly attributable to the interest income earned.





Prayer



It is prayed that the Office be directed to consider and allow the related finance cost of Rs 483,401,279 against Finance income of Rs 139,985,000. Such action has been made totally ignoring the nature of the finance agreements of the company. 

















Ground of Appeal No. 5

The ACIR has erred in rejecting the claim for exemption from tax under clause 141 of Part I of Second Schedule to the Ordinance on the interest income earned on receivable from Sui Southern Gas Company Limited [SSGCL] of Rs 197,288,000 received under the “LNG operations and Services Agreement [LSA]” with SSGCL.





ACIR’s Contentions



The ACIR has yet again reclassified income earned on receivable from SSGCL of Rs 197,288,000 as “Income from Other Sources” under section 39 of the Ordinance on basis that the said interest income is not earned from the business of the entity i.e. terminal establishment and operations. The ACIR has treated this interest income earned on a long term business receivable as similar to the profit on bank and term deposits as discussed in Grounds of Appeal nos. 3 and 4. The ACIR’s contentions on pages 23 and 24 of the Order in this respect are stated as under:



“The taxpayer has claimed that its entire ‘other income’ is ‘Income from business’/ connected to the business as profit on debt has been set off against the financial cost incurred during the year on the subordinated loan’. Further, the taxpayer contends that receivables from SSGCL are ‘on account of construction of a “Branch Pipeline therefore interest income thereon is exempt under clause 141 of Part I of the Second Schedule to the Ordinance as it relates to LNG Operations and Services Agreement [LSA]. As briefly discussed in preceding paragraphs, this proposition is not based on the facts and relevant provisions of the law. Taxpayer’s declarations at note 1 to its audited financial statements and at para 8.1 to its reply strengthens departmental point of view that the taxpayer deals in earning business income from operation of elegy terminal and other allied activities. Furthermore, the taxpayer corporation was found to establish and operate LNG terminal etc. It was not established to earn interest income on Term Deposits, Saving Certificates and receivables. The earning interest income was never a business of the taxpayer. Hence, markup income is chargeable to tax as other income u/s 39 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 and consequently only expenses paid in earning of such income are admissible u/s 40 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001……”





Appellants’ Arguments



The basic contention for the action taken is that the appellant Company has accrued and declared interest income of Rs 197,288,000 on “Long term receivable from SSGCL” as “Income from Business” under section 18 of the Ordinance. The said income was, therefore, claimed as exempt since profits and gains derived by LNG Terminal Operators and Terminal Owners from terminal operations are exempt by virtue of clause 141 of Part I of Second Schedule to the Ordinance: 



“(141)	   Profit and gains derived by LNG Terminal Operators and Terminal Owners for a period of five years beginning from the date when commercial operations are commenced.” 

	

The ACIR has reclassified the said interest income under the head “Income from Other Sources” under section 39 of the Ordinance on similar reasoning as that used for classifying bank and term deposits as an income from other source unrelated to the business of the appellant and subjected the same to tax at the rate of 31 percent. 



This income relates to “Long term receivable from SSGCL” on account of construction of a “Branch Pipeline” undertaken by EETPL as required under the terms of the LSA entered into with SSGCL. This income is identified in note 26 to the financial statements as under:





Reference is made to Note 1 to the Financial Statements wherefrom it is clear that EETPL is further responsible under the LSA for the infrastructure facilities of the terminal for the regasification and delivery of LNG to SSGCL. The said note has been narrated as under:



                    



The SSGCL Branch pipeline was thus specifically required by SSGCL to be a part of the LNG Terminal and therefore, SSGCL had required such construction to be made as part of the LSA terms and conditions. The receivable outstanding represents construction costs incurred on the pipeline which are being recovered periodically from SSGCL. This fact is evident from note 7 to the Financial Statements as reproduced below for your perusal: 







The interest income of Rs 197,288,000 is earned on the “Long Term Receivable” as above and arising out of the LSA is related to the business of the entity i.e. terminal operations and hence claimed as exempt by virtue of clause 141 of Part I of Second Schedule to the Ordinance. 



It is pertinent to mention here that SSGCL is currently the sole consumer of EETPL services of regasification of LNG. The entity was specifically established as a wholly owned subsidiary of ETPL under the Request for Proposal whereby the SSGCL contract was tendered out to EETPL.



Since the interest income relates to the business income of the entity, the same are not to be classified as “Income from Other Sources”. Similar issue has been contested in cases of Power generation companies which are exempt from levy of tax on turnover other than the sale of electricity. In those cases, other receipts under the Power Purchase Agreements inter alia Delayed payment charges, Capacity purchase price and Workers’ Profit Participation Fund and Workers’ Welfare Fund were treated as separate from the “Sale of Electricity” under the Power Purchase Agreement. 

   

We refer to the following cases of the ATIR wherein it has been held that receipts under an exclusive contract, irrespective of their nomenclature, are considered to be of similar character:



ITA 894/LB/2012 dated October 24, 2012 in the case of M/s Lalpir Power Limited and others [copy enclosed as Annexure ‘C’]:



“(vi)   Minimum tax liability



29.	  This matter relates to charge of minimum tax on capacity revenues, interest on delayed payments by WAPDA and supplemental bonus income by the Additional Commissioner while rejecting the taxpayer's claim for exemption from minimum tax under clause (11A)(v) of Part-IV of the Second Schedule to the Ordinance on the plea that such exemption is available only to sale of electricity. Before the first appellate authority, the AR of the taxpayer relied upon the decision of this tribunal in (1999) 80 TAX 71 in which learned members by placing further reliance on the findings of the Supreme Court of India in 1994 PTD 1171 held that where there is an accretion in receipt under the same contract, the nature of the accretion shall remain the same and it will partake the colour of the same receipt on which accretion takes place, irrespective of the fact, whether it takes place directly under the contract or because of some subsequent events so long the source remains the same contract. This proposition has been discussed in the following words in the decision of this Tribunal, relied upon by the taxpayer before the first appellate authority:



"We further agree with the principle laid down by the Indian Supreme Court in the judgment reported as (1994) PTD 1171 (2003 ITR 881) and hold that if there is accretion in receipts under the same contract the nature of accretion shall remain same and it shall partake the colour of same receipts on which accretion takes place, irrespective of the fact whether it takes place directly under the contract or because of some subsequent events so long the source remains the same contract"





30.	The learned LA/DR argued that the first appellate authority erred in extending the exemption to other receipts while dealing with appeal for the tax year 2010. On our query as to whether the receipts on which minimum tax has been imposed by the Additional Commissioner emanate from the same contract whereunder revenue on account of sale accrues to the taxpayer, the learned LA/DR replied in affirmative. In these circumstances, we do not find any infirmity in the findings of the first appellate authority on the issue. It is a fact verifiable from record that the subject receipts, being received under the same power purchase agreement which was entered into for sale of electricity, therefore, the other receipts would partake the same character. In fact, the taxpayer in this case is engaged exclusively in the business of sale of electricity, hence, all other forms of revenue, contemplated in the Power Purchase Agreement, are nothing but consideration for sale of electricity though payable different circumstances/ eventualities. Consequently, in the light of clear finding of this Tribunal, it is our opinion that all receipts under the Power Purchased Agreement would be treated as consideration for sale of electricity and since exemption from levy of minimum tax is undisputedly available to sale revenue, therefore, the same would also apply to other types of revenues. The appeal on this point also fails.” (emphasis is ours)



ITA No. 917/IB/2012 and others dated February 26, 2013 in the case of the Hub Power Company Limited [copy enclosed as Annexure ‘D’]:	



“Considering the above submissions involving both factual and legal merits of the case we find that the issue has been laid to rest by the learned Appellate Tribunal in the case of Lalpir Power Ltd. in ITA No. 894 to 896/LB/2012 and 1147 to 1149/LB/2012. The learned Appellate Tribunal in its order dated 24-10-2012 adjudicated and decided the issue in the following manner -



"Before the first appellate authority, the AR of the taxpayer relied upon the decision of this tribunal in (1999) 80 Tax 71 in which learned members by placing further reliance on the findings of the Supreme Court of India in 1994 PTD 1171 held that where there is an accretion in receipt under the same contract, the nature of the accretion shall remain the same and it will partake the colour of the same receipt on which accretion takes place, irrespective of the fact, whether it takes place directly under the contract or because of some subsequent events so long the source remains the same contract. This proposition has been discussed in the following words in the decision of this Tribunal relied upon by the taxpayer before the first appellate authority:



"We further agree with the principle laid down by the Indian Supreme Court in the judgment reported as (1994) PTD 1171 (2003 ITR 881) and hold that if there is accretion in receipts under the same contract the nature of accretion shall remain same and it shall partake the colour of same receipts on which accretion takes place, irrespective of the fact whether it takes place directly under the contact or because of some subsequent events so long the source remains the same contract."





The learned LA/DR argued that the first appellate authority erred in extending the exemption to other receipts while dealing with appeal for the tax year 2010. On our query as to whether the receipts on which minimum tax has been imposed by the Additional Commissioner emanate from the same contract whereunder revenue on account of sale accrues to the taxpayer, the learned LA/DR replied in affirmative. In these circumstances, we do not find any infirmity in the findings of the first appellate authority on the issue. It is a fact verifiable fro record that the subject receipt, being received under the same power purchase agreement which was entered into for sale of electricity, therefore, the other receipts would partake the same character. In fact, the taxpayer in this case is engaged exclusively in the business of sale of electricity, hence, all other forms of revenue, contemplated in the Power Purchase Agreement, are nothing but consideration for sale of electricity though payable [under] different circumstances / eventualities. Consequently, in the light of clear finding of this Tribunal, it is our opinion that all receipts under the Power Purchase Agreement would be treated as consideration for sale of electricity and since exemption from levy of minimum tax is undisputedly available to sale revenue, therefore, the same would also apply to other types of revenues."



We have found the above decision of the Tribunal to be on all fours of the case of the appellant and therefore, respectfully following the above decision, we allow the appeals filed by the appellant for all the impugned tax years and direct the Deputy Commissioner Inland Revenue to allow the exemption as claimed by the appellant under clause (11) / (11A), Part IV of the Second Schedule to the Ordinance on the impugned receipts in the respective years.”



ITA No. 905/KB/2013 dated March 26, 2016 and ITA No. 489/KB/2015 dated March 19, 2020 in the case of M/s Engro Powergen Qadirpur Ltd [copies enclosed as Annexure ‘E’ and ‘F’]:



	“13. As in the instant case we already observed that the company of the taxpayer commenced and operative on 27-3-2010 which falls under the sphere of clause 132 of Part I of Second Schedule therefore, we are of the view that as per clause 11A (v) the taxpayer's company qualify exemption in terms of clause I of Second Schedule in respect of receipt from sale of electricity.

	

14. Keeping in view the abovementioned prospects in mind we hold that the taxpayer engaged exclusively in the business of sale of electricity so the receipts under the power purchase agreement the exemption from levy of minimum tax is available to sale revenue therefore, the same would also apply to other tax of revenues. The said issues also decided by the Tribunal in ITA No.917 to 921/IB/2012 tax year 2006 to 2011 dated 26-2-2013 and 
ITA No.894 to 896 and 1147 to 1149/LB of 2012 for tax years 2009 to 2011 dated 240-10-2012 wherein the learned Tribunal held that the receipts under whatever nomenclature are covered under power purchase agreement definitely qualify the definition of word 'sale of electricity.' So the said decisions are binding upon this bench therefore, we respectfully following the dictum hold that the impugned order does not require any interference. Resultantly the appeal of the appellant is dismissed.”





Based on the above, you will appreciate that since the Honourable Tribunal has held that receipts under a contract are to be considered similar in nature, the said interest income arising on a long term business receivable of the appellant is rightfully categorized as Business income and consequently exempt under clause 141 of Part I of Second Schedule to the Ordinance.





Prayer 



		From the aforesaid provisions of law and the placing reliance on the decisions of the ATIR, it is prayed that the said interest income of Rs 197,288,000 be allowed as business income of the appellant under the provisions of section 18 of the Ordinance.

APPLICATION FOR STAY OF DEMAND

Brief Facts of the Order and Demand of Tax

1. The subject appeal has been filed under cover of our letter DT 2345 dated December 9, 2022 under 
section 131 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 [Ordinance] against the Appellate Order dated 
November 23, 2022 of the Commissioner Inland Revenue (Appeals-I) [CIR(A)]. 

2. The Order of the CIR(A) disposes off the appeal filed against the Order dated January 29, 2021, framed under section 122(5A) of the Ordinance by the Additional Commissioner Inland Revenue [ACIR], 
Audit – I, Range - B, Large Taxpayers Office, Karachi [hereinafter referred as Impugned Order] where demand of Rs 88,405,132 was maintained on “exparte basis”.
Recovery Proceedings 
3. Recovery proceedings have been initiated by the Deputy Commissioner Inland Revenue, Zone-II, Range-B, Unit 04, Large Taxpayer Office, Karachi and the appellant has been served with a notice dated September 11, 2024, issued under section 138(1) of the Ordinance requiring the payment of demand of 
Rs 88,405,132 by September 12, 2024; copy enclosed as Annexure ‘A’.

4. Since the tax demanded is required to be paid by September 18, 2024, this stay application is being filed and it is prayed that the stay be granted to the appellant till the appeal has been heard and order is passed by the ATIR as the recovery proceedings would cause undue hardship for the appellant as the demand has been incorrectly adjudged for the reasons detailed in the following paragraphs.

Status of Stay from Revenue Authorities

5. Currently, no stay application is pending before any Revenue Authority or Other Authority.

Reasons for the Stay 

6. The CIR(A) has framed the Impugned Order without taking into account the submissions on merit / facts involved on the issues in appeal which were available on record; thus, the Appellate Order, made on an ex-parte basis, is illegal and warrants to be annulled. The details of proceedings are discussed below.
7. Brief facts of the proceedings are as under:

Additional Commissioner Inland Revenue

(a) Amendment proceedings for the year were initiated were initiated vide Show cause notice dated December 2, 2020, issued under section 122(5A) of the Ordinance.

(b) This required certain information / explanations with an intention to amend the assessment deemed under section 120(1) of the Ordinance. This notice was responded vide letter DT 3322 dated January 21, 2021.

(c) The above response was followed by another response vide letter DT 3527 dated January 29, 2021, after discussions with the ACIR on January 26, 2021. No new notice was received after the show cause notice dated December 2, 2020, and the Amended Order dated January 29, 2021, was framed under section 122(5A) of the Ordinance. 

Commissioner Inland Revenue (Appeals)
(d) Stay was applied and allowed by the CIR(A) on March 15, 2021. Stay application included submissions on legal and fact plaints of the disallowances made in the Amended Order dated January 29, 2021, which were made available to the CIR(A). 
(e) Hearing of appeal was fixed vide notices dated March 11, 2021, March 15, 2021, March 11, 2022, and November 15, 2022, on IRIS portal of the FBR; these were not served physically.
(f) On November 23, 2022, the subject Appellate Order was uploaded on IRIS on an ex-parte basis. Again, this Order was also not physically served at the registered address of the appellant.

Factual Submissions on the Impugned Order:
8. Addition has been made for an amount of Rs 337,273,000 under section 39 of the Ordinance considering the same as ‘Interest Income’ chargeable to tax as ‘Income from Other Source’ vis a vis declared exempt income of Rs 1,431,729,540 under Clause 141 of Part I of Second Schedule to the Ordinance. Taxation of Profit on Debt under Section 39 of the Ordinance as “Income from Other Sources”

(v) Consequently, that is the treatment which is reflected in the return whereby the said income was set off against the related finance costs associated with the subordinated and foreign loan of Rs 483,401,279. The said treatment has, however, been considered impermissible by the Officer along with the following comments:

“x. Similarly, the taxpayer’s argument at Para 6.10 that it has set off the said income against the related transactional and other costs associated with the subordinated loan and net finance costs of Rs 649,405,000 i.e. after set off of total finance costs of Rs 139,985,000 with mark-up income; does not carry any weight as the taxpayer is not allowed to set off income chargeable to tax against the expenses incurred to earn exempt income. The law says that a person can claim deduction for business expenses if such expenses have been incurred, wholly or partly, for the purposes of deriving such business income which is chargeable to tax under the provisions of the Income Tax Ordinance 2001. The provisions of section 20(1) of the Ordinance are reproduced as under:…..”

(vi) The Officer has further disallowed the adjustment of said finance costs on subordinated loan from ETPL of Rs 483,401,279 under the provisions of section 40 of the Ordinance against the reclassified profit on debt of Rs 139,985,000 as “Income from Other Sources” under section 39 of the Ordinance. This is on the premise that the subordinated availed was for the purposes of earning income exempt from tax and therefore the related finance costs are business expense. The Officer’s contention in this respect are reproduced below for ready reference:

“d. The finance cost paid/ (payable) by the taxpayer does not fall under the classification of deduction u/s 40 of the Ordinance because the subordinated loan was not availed for earning profit on debt/ ‘Income from Other Sources’; but for deriving business income from operations of LNG terminal which is exempt from tax u/cl. 141 of Part of the Second schedule to the Ordinance. This proposition has been established by the Hon’ Supreme Court of Pakistan in the judgment of Utch Power (Pvt) Ltd cited as 2010 PTD (SC)1809 & by the Hon’ Sindh High Court in the case of Khairatul Amin; cited as (2000) 81 TAX 311 (HC Karachi),= (2000) 
PTD 363.”

Taxation of Interest on Receivable from Sui Southern Gas Company Limited [SSGCL] under Section   39 of the Ordinance as “Income from Other Sources”

(vii) The interest income of Rs 197,288,000 is accrued on a “Long term receivable from SSGCL” on account of construction of a “Branch Pipeline” undertaken by Company as required under the terms of the LNG Operations and Services Agreement [LSA] entered into with SSGCL. (viii) Reference is also made to Note 1.2 to the Financial Statements wherefrom it has been narrated as under:
A Fast Track LNG project tender was issued by Inter State Gas Systems (Private) Limited (ISGS) on
behalf of the Government of Pakistan on August 15, 2013 for receipt, storage and te-gasification of
1.5 million tons of LNG in the first year and 3.0 million tons per annum for the next 14 years. Elengy
Terminal Pakistan Limited (ETPL), the Holding Company, through bidding process was successful to
obtain the contract for the supply of re-gasified LNG to Sui Southern Gas Company Limited (SSGCL).
The Project was subsequently approved by SSGCL Board on November 26, 2013.

Under the Request For Proposal (RFP), ETPL was required to incorporate a special purpose vehicle
which will own and operate the LNG facilities and enter into all Project related agreements including
the LNG Operations and Services Agreement (LSA). On January 9, 2014, the Company was
incorporated as a wholly owned subsidiary of ETPL for this purpose, LSA was formally signed by the
Company with SSGCL on Apri! 30, 2014. The Company, for the purpose of Project, was required to
procure, transport, develop terminal facilities and store and re-gasify LNG under the LSA for a period
of 15 years. This included construction of SSGCL Branch Pipeline to be handed over to SSGCL on
completion for which the Company received Certificate of Acceptance from SSGCL on March 29,
2015. The Company accordingly commenced commercial operations i.e. delivery of regasified LNG to

SSGCL from that date.




(ix) Since the Company is required to provide the services of receiving, storage, regasification and delivery of LNG to SSGCL under the terms of the LSA alongwith provision and maintenance of requisite LNG Services Infrastructure for provisions of the services as stated in the Contract. The receivable outstanding hence represents construction costs incurred on the pipeline which are being recovered periodically from SSGCL. This fact is further evident from note 7 to the Financial Statements as reproduced below for your convenience:

As stated in note 1.2, the Company entered into LSA with SSGCL. As per the terms of LSA, the
Company was required to construct / build SSGC Branch Pipeline to be transferred to SSGCL upon
commissioning of the Project. The Company under the LSA is entitled to recover the cost of
construction through charges to be billed to SSGCL over the term of LSA. The Company constructed
and transferred the SSGC Branch Pipeline to SSGCL on March 29, 2015, for which the Certificate of
Acceptance has been received from SSGCL. The receivable represents construction costs incurred in

this respect net of recoveries.




(x) Consequently, entire receipts under the LSA are exempt as part of profits and gains derived by LNG Terminal Operators and Terminal Owners under clause 141 of Part I of Second Schedule to the Ordinance. 

(xi) Reliance was also placed on precedents wherein similar matters have been raised and adjudicated in the case of Power generation companies which are exempt from levy of tax on turnover other than the sale of electricity. Following cases have referred wherein other receipts under the Power Purchase Agreements interalia Delayed payment charges, Capacity purchase price and Workers’ Profit Participation Fund and Workers’ Welfare Fund were treated as separate from the “Sale of Electricity” under the Power Purchase Agreement:

(a) ITA 894/LB/2012 dated October 24, 2012, in the case of M/s Lalpir Power Limited and others;

(b) ITA No. 917/IB/2012 and others dated February 26, 2013, in the case of the Hub Power Company Limited; and

(c) ITA No. 905/KB/2013 dated March 26, 2016, and ITA No. 489/KB/2015 dated March 19, 2020 in the case of M/s Engro Powergen Qadirpur Ltd.

(xii) The Officer has, however, through this Order has refuted the explanations provided and bifurcated the said interest income earned on the long term receivable from SSGCL from its principal amount and hence separately taxed the said interest income as “Income from Other Sources” under section 39 of the Ordinance. The Officer’s comments pertaining to this matter on page 22 of the Order are reproduced below:

“By taxpayer’s own declaration, ‘this account is accrued on receivable due from SSGCL to EETPL. This income relates to “Long term receivable from SSGCL”. Thus, the amount of Rs. 197,288,000/- is on account of receivables from SSGCL i.e on account of taxpayer’s money being utilized by SSGCL. Had this money been kept into savings account or had it been given as loan to any other business entity/ person, the same would have entitled the taxpayer to receipt of interest. Therefore, Interest on receivable from Sui Southern Gas Company Limited [SSGCL]’ for all purposes is profit on debt.”

Prayer

10. This demand has been raised on gross misapplication of law in the case of the company and being unreasonable is not acceptable. The recovery thereof, would cause irreparable loss to the appellant.

11. Based on facts and circumstances of the case relating to the issue under appeal, favorable decisions, allowing relief to the appellant are expected in the instant case, meaning thereby, the balance of convenience is in favour of the appellant. There is a ‘prima-facie’ case for grant of stay from recovery of the tax demand till the matter is decided by the Honorable Tribunal. Moreover, if the department is allowed to recover the said demand, it would result in irreparable loss to the applicant.

(v) Consequently, that is the treatment which is reflected in the return whereby the said income was set off against the related finance costs associated with the subordinated and foreign loan of Rs 483,401,279. The said treatment has, however, been considered impermissible by the Officer along with the following comments:

“x. Similarly, the taxpayer’s argument at Para 6.10 that it has set off the said income against the related transactional and other costs associated with the subordinated loan and net finance costs of Rs 649,405,000 i.e. after set off of total finance costs of Rs 139,985,000 with mark-up income; does not carry any weight as the taxpayer is not allowed to set off income chargeable to tax against the expenses incurred to earn exempt income. The law says that a person can claim deduction for business expenses if such expenses have been incurred, wholly or partly, for the purposes of deriving such business income which is chargeable to tax under the provisions of the Income Tax Ordinance 2001. The provisions of section 20(1) of the Ordinance are reproduced as under:…..”

(vi) The Officer has further disallowed the adjustment of said finance costs on subordinated loan from ETPL of Rs 483,401,279 under the provisions of section 40 of the Ordinance against the reclassified profit on debt of Rs 139,985,000 as “Income from Other Sources” under section 39 of the Ordinance. The Officer’s contention in this respect are reproduced below for ready reference:

“d. A Fast Track LNG project tender was issued by Inter State Gas Systems (Private) Limited (ISGS) on
behalf of the Government of Pakistan on August 15, 2013 for receipt, storage and te-gasification of
1.5 million tons of LNG in the first year and 3.0 million tons per annum for the next 14 years. Elengy
Terminal Pakistan Limited (ETPL), the Holding Company, through bidding process was successful to
obtain the contract for the supply of re-gasified LNG to Sui Southern Gas Company Limited (SSGCL).
The Project was subsequently approved by SSGCL Board on November 26, 2013.

Under the Request For Proposal (RFP), ETPL was required to incorporate a special purpose vehicle
which will own and operate the LNG facilities and enter into all Project related agreements including
the LNG Operations and Services Agreement (LSA). On January 9, 2014, the Company was
incorporated as a wholly owned subsidiary of ETPL for this purpose, LSA was formally signed by the
Company with SSGCL on Apri! 30, 2014. The Company, for the purpose of Project, was required to
procure, transport, develop terminal facilities and store and re-gasify LNG under the LSA for a period
of 15 years. This included construction of SSGCL Branch Pipeline to be handed over to SSGCL on
completion for which the Company received Certificate of Acceptance from SSGCL on March 29,
2015. The Company accordingly commenced commercial operations i.e. delivery of regasified LNG to

SSGCL from that date.




(ix) Since the Company is required to provide the services of receiving, storage, regasification and delivery of LNG to SSGCL under the terms of the LSA alongwith provision and maintenance of requisite LNG Services Infrastructure for provisions of the services as stated in the Contract. construction through charges to be billed to SSGCL over the term of LSA. The Company constructed

this respect net of recoveries.

Following cases have referred wherein other receipts under the Power Purchase Agreements interalia Delayed payment charges, Capacity purchase price and Workers’ Profit Participation Fund and Workers’ Welfare Fund were treated as separate from the “Sale of Electricity” under the Power Purchase Agreement:

(a) ITA 894/LB/2012 dated October 24, 2012, in the case of M/s Lalpir Power Limited and others;

(b) ITA No. 917/IB/2012 and others dated February 26, 2013, in the case of the Hub Power Company Limited; and

(c) ITA No. 905/KB/2013 dated March 26, 2016, and ITA No. 489/KB/2015 dated March 19, 2020 in the case of M/s Engro Powergen Qadirpur Ltd.

(xii) The Officer has, however, through this Order has refuted the explanations provided and bifurcated the said interest income earned on the long term receivable from SSGCL from its principal amount and hence separately taxed the said interest income as “Income from Other Sources” under section 39 of the Ordinance. The Officer’s comments pertaining to this matter on page 22 of the Order are reproduced below:

“By taxpayer’s own declaration, ‘this account is accrued on receivable due from SSGCL to EETPL. This income relates to “Long term receivable from SSGCL”. Thus, the amount of Rs. 197,288,000/- is on account of receivables from SSGCL i.e on account of taxpayer’s money being utilized by SSGCL. Had this money been kept into savings account or had it been given as loan to any other business entity/ person, the same would have entitled the taxpayer to receipt of interest. Therefore, Interest on receivable from Sui Southern Gas Company Limited [SSGCL]’ for all purposes is profit on debt.”

Prayer

10. This demand has been raised on gross misapplication of law in the case of the company and being unreasonable is not acceptable. The recovery thereof, would cause irreparable loss to the appellant.

11. Based on facts and circumstances of the case relating to the issue under appeal, favorable decisions, allowing relief to the appellant are expected in the instant case, meaning thereby, the balance of convenience is in favour of the appellant. There is a ‘prima-facie’ case for grant of stay from recovery of the tax demand till the matter is decided by the Honorable Tribunal. Moreover, if the department is allowed to recover the said demand, it would result in irreparable loss to the applicant. 

12. It is therefore prayed that the Honourable Tribunal kindly grant stay of demand as recovery of tax levied under this Ordinance shall cause undue hardship to the taxpayer.

M/s Getz Pharma (Pvt.) Limited, a manufacturer, importer, and marketer of pharmaceutical products, faced a penalty under Section 182(1) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, for allegedly failing to pay 90% of its advance tax liability as required under Section 147 for the tax year 2018. The penalty of Rs. 11,052,299 was based on a shortfall in advance tax payments. A thorough review of the case establishes that this penalty is unjustified, being rooted in procedural errors by the tax department and contrary to the principles of justice and fairness.

The core issue originates from the mismanagement of sales tax refunds issued as Refund Payment Orders (RPOs). The Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) admitted in its letter dated November 29, 2018, that these RPOs, intended for adjustment against advance tax under Section 147, were mistakenly deposited under sales tax. This error precluded the taxpayer from using the refunds to meet its advance tax obligations. The department explicitly instructed the taxpayer not to adjust these amounts for tax year 2018, instead permitting adjustments in subsequent years. Consequently, the shortfall in advance tax payments was a direct result of the department’s own mistake, which was acknowledged but not rectified. This context negates any assertion that the taxpayer deliberately failed to meet its obligations.

In response to the show-cause notice, the taxpayer provided a detailed explanation supported by evidence. The taxpayer highlighted that the shortfall arose from the misapplied refunds and referenced prior appellate rulings where similar penalties were overturned due to departmental errors. Despite this, the Deputy Commissioner Inland Revenue (DCIR) proceeded to impose the penalty, dismissing the taxpayer’s explanation without adequately addressing the acknowledged error or the taxpayer’s lack of intent. The DCIR’s conclusion that the taxpayer’s actions constituted willful non-compliance is unsustainable given the circumstances.

The taxpayer’s conduct reflects consistent efforts to address the issue in good faith. Multiple communications, including letters dated March 2, 2018, March 15, 2018, and November 28, 2018, were sent to the department, highlighting the error and seeking rectification. These actions demonstrate that the taxpayer acted responsibly and with the intention of compliance. Judicial precedents, such as the ruling in 102 TAX 443, emphasize that taxpayers cannot be penalized for defaults caused by the tax authorities’ procedural lapses. This principle applies directly to the present case, where the shortfall resulted solely from the department’s error.

The absence of mens rea further invalidates the imposition of the penalty. Established legal principles require proof of intent or gross negligence to impose penalties under Section 182(1). The taxpayer’s submissions clearly demonstrate that the shortfall was neither deliberate nor attributable to any negligence on its part. The taxpayer relied on the department’s instructions and could not have anticipated or mitigated the impact of the erroneous refund adjustments. Judicial rulings have consistently upheld that penalties cannot be imposed without evidence of intent, a condition absent in this case.

The imposition of the penalty also disregards prior appellate decisions that favored the taxpayer in similar circumstances. The Commissioner Appeals, in a decision dated December 30, 2019, held that penalties or additional liabilities could not be imposed where compliance was impeded by errors attributable to the department. This precedent further supports the taxpayer’s position and underscores the inconsistency in the DCIR’s decision.

The taxpayer’s case is strengthened by the FBR’s own acknowledgment of its procedural lapses. The department admitted that the RPOs were misapplied and directed the taxpayer not to adjust the refunds for tax year 2018. Penalizing the taxpayer under these circumstances contradicts the principles of equity and justice. The penalty computation also failed to consider the impact of the misapplied refunds, further highlighting the procedural flaws in the DCIR’s order.

Given these findings, it is evident that the penalty imposed under Section 182(1) lacks both legal and factual basis. The shortfall in advance tax payments was caused entirely by the department’s error, and the taxpayer cannot be held liable for circumstances beyond its control. The absence of intent, combined with prior appellate rulings and judicial precedents, reinforces the conclusion that the penalty is unwarranted. The taxpayer acted in good faith, complied with procedural requirements, and consistently engaged with the department to address the issue.

The appeal is allowed, and the penalty imposed under Section 182(1) is set aside. The department is directed to rectify its procedural errors and ensure that similar issues do not recur. This decision upholds the principles of fairness, justice, and accountability, ensuring that taxpayers are not unjustly penalized for errors attributable to the tax authorities.

### Facts of the Case:

1. **Nature of Business**:
   - The taxpayer, M/s Getz Pharma (Pvt.) Limited, is engaged in manufacturing, importing, and marketing pharmaceutical and auxiliary products. The registered office is in Korangi Industrial Area, Karachi.

2. **Penalty under Section 182(1)**:
   - The taxpayer was penalized for paying less than 90% of the tax payable under Section 147 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, as computed in the deemed assessment order for the tax year 2018. The penalty imposed amounts to Rs. 11,052,299.

3. **Dispute Regarding Adjustment of Sales Tax Refunds**:
   - Refund Payment Orders (RPOs) issued for sales tax were incorrectly deposited under sales tax instead of being adjusted under Section 147 for advance tax liability. This mistake was acknowledged by the tax department in its letter dated November 29, 2018【11†source】.
   - The department directed the taxpayer not to adjust these amounts for the tax year 2018 but allowed adjustments in subsequent years【11†source】.

4. **Previous Commissioner Appeals Order**:
   - In an earlier appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that the taxpayer could not be penalized for the department's mistake regarding the adjustment of sales tax refunds【10†source】.

5. **Findings in the Current Impugned Order**:
   - The Deputy Commissioner Inland Revenue (DCIR) concluded that the taxpayer failed to discharge its advance tax liability, which constitutes deliberate and willful default. The penalty was imposed despite the taxpayer's submission of earlier appellate decisions and relevant documentation【9†source】【10†source】.

6. **Taxpayer’s Contentions**:
   - The taxpayer argues that:
     - The penalty is unjustified as sales tax refunds were erroneously adjusted due to the department's fault.
     - Penalty under Section 182(1) cannot be imposed without establishing mens rea, as upheld in judicial precedents.
     - Advance tax payments were impacted by the department’s instructions not to adjust certain amounts【8†source】【10†source】.

### Positive Findings as Commissioner Appeals:

1. **Departmental Fault**:
   - The incorrect adjustment of sales tax refunds was a departmental error, acknowledged in the FBR's letter. This error led to shortfalls in advance tax payments, and the taxpayer should not be penalized for the department’s mistake.

2. **Absence of Mens Rea**:
   - Judicial precedents require establishing intent (mens rea) for imposing penalties. The absence of deliberate intent by the taxpayer negates the basis for the penalty under Section 182(1).

3. **Established Precedent**:
   - Earlier appellate orders have favored the taxpayer on similar grounds, directing recalculation or deletion of liabilities where departmental errors impacted tax compliance【10†source】.

4. **Legislative and Procedural Compliance**:
   - Section 182(1) and Section 147 aim to ensure compliance, but procedural lapses by tax authorities should not translate into punitive measures against taxpayers who acted in good faith.

5. **Taxpayer’s Cooperation**:
   - The taxpayer has consistently communicated and complied with departmental notices, including submitting explanations and participating in hearings.

### Conclusion:

The penalty imposed under Section 182(1) should be revisited. Given the department's acknowledged error and the lack of willful default, the penalty is unjustified. It is recommended that the taxpayer’s appeal be allowed, the penalty order set aside, and procedural adjustments made to prevent recurrence of similar issues.

officer passed the impugned order. The appellant being aggrieved of that

reproduced below:

or (6) of section 147 or the tax so paid is less than ninety per cent of the tax chargeable for 
the relevant tax year, he shall be liable to pay default surcharge at the rate of 12 per cent 
per annum on the amount of tax so chargeable or the amount by which the tax paid by him 
Jalls short of the ninety per cent, as the case may be; and such default surcharge shall be 

calculated from the first day of April in that year to the date on which assessment is made 
or the thirtieth day of June of the financial year next following, whichever is the earlier 

"Provided that in the case of person having a special tax year, the default surcharge shall 
be calculated on and from the first day of the fourth quarter of the special tax year till the 
date on which assessment is made or the last day of special tax year, whichever is earlier."

us. Our special tax year relevant to the appeal is 2018 and tax can be levied from the first

day of the fourth quarter of the special tax year i.e. 01-10-2018 till the date on which

4. I have considered the written and verbal submissions of the AR of the 

appellant and perused the impugned order. My findings on the issues are as 

follows: 

4.1 The dispute in this appeal is regarding ascertainment of number of 

days of default is to be worked out for purpose of levy- of default surcharge 

u/s.205(1B) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001. I have noted the 

contention of the learned AR was rejected by the learned officer by 

observing as under:- 

“It is clear from the above mentioned provision of law that the default is to be calculated 
from the first day of 4" quarter till the filing of the return, or the last day of the next 
financial year, whichever is earlier. It is clear from the above that the total days af default 
comes to. 452 days and not 88 days as submitted by the AR of the taxpayer in the appeal. 
The contention of the taxpayer that the provision to the Section 205(1h) does not mention 
the end of next year is also not tenable because it has been clearly written in the subsection 
itself “to the date on which assessment is made or the thirtieth day of June of the financial 
year next following, whichever is the earlier” for the cases having normal tax year, and 
even if the same has not been repeated in the proviso, the intent of the law is clear that the 
default surcharge is tobe calculated from the first day of the last quarter, till the filing of 
return, or the last day of next financial year whichever is earlier. The taxpayer’s 
interpretation of the law is not correct on this point.” 

4.2 The learned officer while arriving on above conclusion has also 

referred to section 205(1B) which for the sake of facility and ready reference 

is reproduced here as under:- 

“(1B) Where, in respect of any tax year, any taxpayer fails to pay tax un 
(4A), or (6) of section 147 or the tax so paid is less than ninety pe Cet ‘of the the Hex 
chargeable for the relevant tax year, he shall be liable to pay defaul ebrye at the rate’. 
of 12 percent per annum on the amount of tax so chargeable or the mount by which the tax’ \ 
paid by him falls short of the 3 ninety percent, as the case m

Provided that in the case of person having a special tax year, the default surcharge shall be 
calculated on and from the first day of the fourth quarter of the special tax year till the date 
on which assessment is made or the last day of special tax year, whichever is earlier.” 

4.3 On perusal of above provision of law, it reveals that for ascertainment 

of number of days of default for levy of default surcharge, the working is 

required to be calculated from the 1° day of April in that year to the date on 

which assessment is made or 30" June of the financial year next following 

whichever is earlier, this working is in respect of taxpayer following normal 

tax year ending on June 30". Whereas proviso to the above provisions 

caters for persons following special tax year wherein default surcharge is 

worked out from the first day of the fourth quarter till the date of 

assessment order passed or last day of special tax year whichever is earlier. 

The language of this provision is clear where terminal date of calculating 

default surcharge is last day of special tax year. The learned officer erred in 

extending such terminal date provided in the proviso to the end of financial 

year next following on any analogy. When the said date is not provided in 

the proviso applicable for persons following special tax year, then such 

intendment is not allowed to sustain. Therefore, the action of the learned 

officer is not endorsed on this issue. The learned officer is therefore directed 

to re-calculate the subject liability accordingly if warranted. 

4.4 The next issue contended is regarding treatment accorded to the 

outstanding sales tax refunds to be adjusted against the advance tax 

liability. The learned AR produced copy of letter of learned DCIR vide No,167__ 

dated 29.11.2018 wherein the learned officer admitted that refu J oheques 

were to be deposited u/s.147 of the Income Tax Ordinancey/2001 which 

were deposited under sales tax PSIDs and appellant was directed not to 

adjust the amount u/s.137 for tax year 2018. i»

4.5 I have noted that the appellant requested the concerned 

Commissioner for the adjustment of its sales tax refund against advance tax 

liability u/s.147 for tax year 2018. The learned officer in the impugned order 

has observed that the appellant was aware of fact that sales tax refund was 

wrongly adjusted since, September 2017. That the appellant before the start 

of last quarter knew that the refund cheques were not available for 

adjustment against tax liability for tax year 2018. That now, the appellant is 

taking plea that refund of sales tax was available for adjustment which is 

incorrect. The appellant in such circumstances was required to discharge its 

statutory liability in time without waiting for adjustment of sales tax refund 

which was not available and had already been inadvertently adjusted. 

Admittedly, the subject refund RPO’s instead of being adjusted against 

advance income tax u/s.147 for tax year 2018 were now adjusted against 

advance income tax of 2020 due to the fault on the part of the department. 

This resulted in short payment of Advance tax liability for tax year 2018 as 

worked out by the appellant due to non-adjustment of said refund cheque. 

Since, the said default cannot be attributed to the appellant, hence levy of 

default surcharge on such default is held to be unjustified which is also 

directed to be deleted.

APPELLATE ORDER U/S 129 OF THE INCOME TAX ORDINANCE, 2001.

1.
This appeal is filed against the order passed under section 182(2) of the come Tax Ordinance 2001 passed by Deputy Commissioner Inland Revenue, Unit-05, Zone-II, Large Taxpayer Office, LTO, Karachi vide barcode No. 100000198984896 dated: 25.06.2024 for tax year-2018. The following grounds of appeal:
1. That the order passed u/s. 182(1) of the Income Tax Ordinance 2001 by the learned Deputy Commissioner Inland Revenue (DCIR), Unit - 5, Zone-II, LTO, Karachi is bad in law and on facts of the case.

2. That the learned DCIR has erred in charging penalty u/s 182(1) (Serial No 5) of the I.T. Ord. 2001.
3. That the learned DCIR has erred in ignoring the fact that in the instant year under the same facts levy of default surcharge u/s 205(1B) was deleted by Commissioner Appeals vide order 14/A-1 dated 30-12-2019. Copy of the order is attached.

4. That the learned DCIR has erred in ignoring the fact that the tax payer had sales tax refunds through RPOs issued which were to be adjusted against tax u/s 147. But the cheques received by Commissioner Office were wrongly deposited under sales tax which was the fault of the department. Copy of the letter issued by the Commissioner vide letter No CIR/Zone-1/LTU/2018/167 dated 29-11-2018 is attached.
5. That the learned DCIR has erred by not adding wrong depositing of Sales Tax refunds cheques u/s 147 of the I.T. Ord. 2001. The mistake was done by the department for which taxpayer cannot be penalized.  This is settled in judgment reported as (2010) 102 TAX 443 (Trib.)

6. That the learned DCIR has neither established nor attempted to establish mens rea which is a mandatory requirement for imposition of penalty as held in various judgements of superior courts. PLD 1967 SC. 2007 PTD 901 Sindh High Court.
7. That the learned DCIR has erred in ignoring the fact that in the return of income there was a tax refundable.

8. That the learned DCIR in the impugned computation has included FTR tax for calculation the liability u/s 147 which is against clause (d) of sub section 1 of section 147 of the Income Tax ordinance 2001.

9. That the appellant craves permission to add alter or amend any grounds of appeal before the date of hearing………….”

The registered office of the Company is located at 29-30/27, Korangi Industrial Area, Karachi.
Call notices under section 128 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 were issued both sides. None appeared from department’s side. While Mr. S.M Rehan, FCA, as A.R. of the appellant attended and argued the case.
